newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: KPN split idea wins analysts' approval.
newsitem.headline: KPN split idea wins analysts' approval.

text.p: Telecoms analysts on Wednesday welcomed remarks from Koninklijke PTT Nederland (KPN) that it was pondering the separation of its post and telecoms arms, but said any move might be years away.

KPN earlier confirmed comments in a newspaper interview with chairman Wim Dik that the firm was considering a scenario under which KPN would become a holding company for separately traded postal and telecommunication units.

Analysts say this could allow PTT Telecom and PTT Post to develop separately on the international stage, pursuing ventures in their own fields with transparent structures which are immediately understandable to potential partners.

"You cannot really put those two together any more from an investment viewpoint. You either want to invest in a telecoms player or a postal player with a relatively low but healthy growth outlook," said Eric de Graaf of ING Barings.

"In our view it's not impossible that the telecom part will form a joint venture with other companies or will even be taken over by a bigger competitor outside of the Netherlands and they certainly don't want the postal division to be included in anything like that," said De Graaf.
He added that splitting the two companies would be a signal to investors that it was looking ahead and taking the necessary steps to make joint ventures easier.

KPN's successful bid for Australian transport company TNT Ltd is seen more than doubling KPN's annual postal revenues to around 13 billion guilders and has raised KPN's profile as a key global postal player.
The acquisition is beginning to change investors' view of the postal unit as its revenues come into balance with telecoms revenues -- although PTT Telecom has by far the higher profitability.
"Until now it was telecom with a bit of post. After TNT the divisions are the same size in turnover -- it makes for two stand-alone companies who are big enough to mean something," said De Graaf.
"Now they've entered into the TNT deal they have something to focus on, to increase their market share. They're not just the local Dutch postman any more. It's getting a more global size," he added.
But integrating TNT could take years, while international telecoms markets developments point to blockbuster mergers later rather than sooner.

"In the future, and I'm not talking about the next few years, let's say within five to 10 years, joint ventures will be the name of the game in telecoms, look at BT and MCI," said De Graaf, referring to British Telecommunications Plc's and MCI Communications Corp's planned merger.

"It's undoubted that there will be further concentrations in the telecoms market," said HSBC Van Meer James Capel analyst Joost van Beek. "I think KPN has a stronger position in concluding alliances if it's just a clean telecoms company."
He added that a stand-alone postal company would also be well placed to capitalise on any future liberalisation of the postal market.

"Now with the TNT acquisition, in terms of size, it's comparable to telecoms. But a lot of restructuring needs to be done at TNT and that's a process which will take at least two to three years, and I don't think it would be wise to go for a demerger before the TNT acquisition is fully integrated and paying off," said Van Beek.
Analysts said there was little to be gained operationally by splitting the company while it remained to be seen whether the split would improve yields to current shareholders.
"The moment you get a takeover story, shares go up and so shareholder value goes up. From an operating point of view there is no clear advantage," said De Graaf.

"It's more that they open up possiblities for joint ventures. If they want to team up with another big telecoms company, that firm would not be interested in buying into the postal division as well," he said.
